standfirst: Twenty-four episodes on the years Korea lost its sovereignty, told through a Korean-American marine, a noblewoman running guns and two men who love her without hope. Nothing has matched it, which is why this page is a list of near misses rather than replacements. Two honest warnings. Kim Eun-sook writes in a deliberately poetic, elliptical register that reads as a wall if you are not in the mood for it, and the romance is chaste to the point of frustration: they never even get a kiss.

picks.why: The closest anyone gets to the yearning at this scale. Twenty-one episodes of two people separated by an invasion, with the same conviction that history is a character and it does not negotiate. The same restraint too: longing carried in glances and withheld sentences rather than declarations. Difference: it does technically end happily, and it charges you across two seasons to get there. Mr. Sunshine never offers that deal.

The same argument in twelve episodes instead of twenty-four: two people meeting at the exact moment their country is about to do something unforgivable. Golden, unbearably pretty, and structured so that you know roughly what is coming and cannot stop watching anyway. Difference: 1980 rather than 1900, much smaller in scope, and it hurts faster.

For the love that duty will not permit. A king who chooses one woman and a woman who keeps choosing her own freedom instead, played with the same restraint and the same understanding that a hand not taken is the whole scene. Difference: Joseon palace politics rather than colonial history, and the political plotting is the weakest part rather than the strongest.

If what actually moved you was the resilience rather than the rifles. Decades of Korean twentieth-century hardship carried by ordinary people who keep going, with the same belief that endurance is the story worth telling. Difference: it is domestic and intimate, no colonial occupation and no armed resistance, and it is kind to you in a way Mr. Sunshine never is.

For the doomed-grandeur register in a sageuk. Power won at the direct expense of love, twenty episodes of political manoeuvring, and a finale built to hurt that succeeds. Difference: the first four episodes are genuinely choppy from re-editing, and the fantasy framing is nothing like Mr. Sunshine's documentary seriousness about real events.

The modern-dress version of the same thesis: that the times can simply overrule two people who were right for each other. Same use of a national crisis as the thing that decides a private life. Difference: it is a coming-of-age drama about fencing and friendship, so the scale and the stakes are ordinary. The ache is the only shared component.

against.title: Goblin
against.why: The automatic pick: same writer, same lush visual grammar. But Goblin is a fantasy romance about immortality and fate, with a comic ensemble and a bright pop soundtrack. Mr. Sunshine is about a real occupation and real dead people. Same pen, opposite contract with the viewer.

against.title: Crash Landing on You
against.why: Suggested as the other epic Korean romance with a political border between the leads. CLOY is engineered so that you land safely and it is very funny on the way. Mr. Sunshine's entire subject is that some things do not work out. Watching one to recover from the other works. Watching one as a replacement does not.

against.title: Empress Ki
against.why: Turns up as the other long, serious historical epic. It is fifty-one episodes of court intrigue in a different century, driven by ambition and palace faction rather than by national survival. The length is comparable, the subject is not.
